title: #1169 - Elon Musk
why: Musk lit up a joint on camera during a rambling late-night conversation, sparking global headlines and a same-day slide in Tesla's share price.

title: 640: Five Women
why: Five women who were harassed by the same boss dissect how their own histories shaped their reactions, a standout #MeToo-era hour that critics ranked among the year's best.

title: Punk Style: Articles of Interest #6
why: The finale of Avery Trufelman's clothing miniseries traced how punk fashion went from DIY rebellion to mall merchandise, and Vulture named it one of 2018's top episodes.

title: The House that Came in the Mail
why: A charming history of Sears mail-order kit homes that made critics' best-episode lists and was later re-aired by popular demand.

title: The Johnlock Conspiracy
why: Willa Paskin's deep dive into Sherlock fans convinced Holmes and Watson were secretly a couple became a widely shared look at fandom gone conspiratorial.

title: The Incunabula Papers
why: A Decoder Ring investigation into a strange cultural puzzle that critics picked as one of the best podcast episodes of 2018.

title: Louis, Can of Cola
why: The debut of an improvised series where an inanimate object is interviewed in earnest landed on Vulture's top episodes and announced a genuinely new podcast format.

title: 'Michael Clayton' With Chris Ryan, Justin Charity, and Lindsay Zoladz
why: A Ringer movie-rewatch session that Vulture's critics picked as one of the ten best episodes of 2018.

title: #127 The Crime Machine, Part I
why: The opening half of a two-parter exposing how NYPD's CompStat numbers drove quota policing, often cited as some of the show's best reporting.

title: #130 The Snapchat Thief
why: A gripping hunt for the person hijacking a teen's Snapchat account that became one of the show's most-recommended mysteries.

title: Charles Oakley Tells MJ Stories, Explains Why LeBron Will Leave, and Remembers His Favorite Fights (And It's Amazing) | The Bill Simmons Podcast (Ep. 375)
why: Oakley's unfiltered tales of Jordan, fights and the NBA made this a viral sports-pod favorite and a year-end list pick.

title: The Red Line
why: An NPR Embedded episode that critics named among the best podcast episodes of 2018.

title: Will Hays and "Pre-Code" Hollywood (Fake News: Fact-Checking Hollywood Babylon Episode 7)
why: Karina Longworth's myth-busting look at Hollywood's censorship czar was cited by critics as a highlight of her acclaimed Hollywood Babylon season.

title: Recode Decode: Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg
why: Zuckerberg's comments to Kara Swisher that Facebook wouldn't remove Holocaust deniers' posts triggered an international backlash and a public walk-back.

title: Introducing “Caliphate,” a New York Times Audio Series
why: The launch of the Times' ISIS series, which won a Peabody before the paper conceded in 2020 that its central source's story didn't hold up and gave the award back.

title: S2 E1: July 16, 1996
why: The opener of APM's Curtis Flowers investigation, a Peabody-winning season whose reporting fed into the Supreme Court overturning his conviction.

title: The Hug Heard Round the World
why: A Malcolm Gladwell history episode about a single televised embrace and what it revealed about its era, chosen as one of 2018's standout episodes.

title: Googling Strangers and Kentucky Bluegrass
why: John Green's tender star-rated reflections on searching for a stranger online and on lawn grass made Vulture's top ten episodes of the year.

title: #1245 - Andrew Yang
why: A long-shot candidate's universal-basic-income pitch went viral here, and his campaign's daily donations jumped dramatically in the following month.

title: #1315 - Bob Lazar & Jeremy Corbell
why: Lazar's UFO claims inspired the 'Storm Area 51' Facebook event that drew millions of RSVPs and became a summer-long meme.

title: #1330 - Bernie Sanders
why: Sanders' sit-down led Rogan to say he'd probably vote for him, a remark the campaign promoted and the press debated during the 2020 primary.

title: 688: The Out Crowd
why: Its reporting on asylum seekers stranded by the Remain in Mexico policy won the first-ever Pulitzer Prize for Audio Reporting.

title: #140 The Roman Mars Mazda Virus
why: A comic tech mystery about a car stereo that crashed whenever it tried to play 99% Invisible, regularly listed among the show's best.

title: Introducing ‘1619,’ a New York Times Audio Series
why: The start of the audio companion to the 1619 Project, which reframed American history around slavery, topped Time's 2019 list and fueled a national debate.

title: Sad Ass Songs
why: The premiere of Jad Abumrad's Peabody-winning series about why Dolly Parton unites a divided country.

title: 146: Disney’s Most Controversial Film (Six Degrees of Song of the South, Episode 1)
why: The first chapter of Longworth's study of Disney's buried 1946 film, a season The Atlantic listed among 2019's best podcasts.

title: #158 The Case of the Missing Hit
why: The hunt for a half-remembered '90s song nobody could find became a phenomenon, with the show's audience reportedly jumping about a third right after it aired.

title: Community with Barack Obama
why: The former first lady's Spotify debut featured her husband as the first guest, and its release made news well beyond podcast circles.

title: 1: The Book of Statuses
why: Chana Joffe-Walt's opener on how white parents shape public schools started one of 2020's most-discussed series and topped Time's episode list.

title: Is It Time To Say R.I.P. To 'POC'?
why: An examination of whether 'people of color' still works as a catch-all term, picked by Time in the same year Apple named Code Switch its show of the year.

title: “It wasn’t sexism, then” (Polly Platt, The Invisible Woman, Episode 1)
why: The opening episode of a season restoring the overlooked production designer Polly Platt to film history, named one of 2020's best by Time.

title: The Next Year (or Two) of the Pandemic
why: Donald McNeil Jr.'s sobering early forecast of how long COVID-19 would last became one of the year's most-cited news episodes.

title: Antediluvian
why: The opener of The Atlantic's Peabody-winning Hurricane Katrina series, also on Time's best episodes of 2020.

title: 01: He's Having Second Thoughts
why: Actor Connor Ratliff's funny, obsessive inquiry into why Tom Hanks fired him from a tiny role kicked off a cult-hit series.

title: 6. A Depression Where I Am
why: A candid lockdown conversation about mental health from Kumail Nanjiani and Emily V. Gordon that Time ranked among 2020's best.

title: Thanksgiving, Part 1: Sage Wisdom (with Demi Adejuyigbe)
why: Samin Nosrat and Hrishikesh Hirway's pandemic cooking show at its warmest, chosen by Time as a top episode of the year.

title: Remember How Messy Top Model Was? (with Jay Manuel)
why: A juicy behind-the-scenes look back at America's Next Top Model that rode the show's 2020 nostalgia reckoning onto Time's list.

title: #1509 - Abigail Shrier
why: Released as Rogan moved to Spotify, it led staff to protest the platform internally, and Spotify's CEO publicly defended keeping it up.

title: #1554 - Kanye West
why: Kanye's marathon talk about his longshot presidential bid made headlines weeks before the 2020 election.

title: An Examination of Caliphate
why: The New York Times' on-air reckoning with the flawed reporting behind its own award-winning series, a rare public correction that dominated media news.

title: A Friendly Ghost Story
why: An inquiry into a family who believes a ghost lives in their house, which Apple named one of its Episodes of the Year.

title: Bubba Wallace
why: Shannon Sharpe's frank conversation with NASCAR's only full-time Black Cup driver, one of Apple's 2021 Episodes of the Year.

title: Glorious Basterds
why: One of the true-life stories Seth Rogen turned into a polished audio comedy-documentary, picked by Apple as a top episode of 2021.

title: How Do I Love Someone?
why: A personal episode from Megan Tan's LAist Studios series on modern love and relationships, which Apple selected as an Episode of the Year.

title: My Parents, Ellen and Tom
why: A deeply personal documentary episode about the creator's own parents, named an Apple Episode of the Year and from a series on The Atlantic's best of 2021.

title: The Body Mass Index
why: Aubrey Gordon and Michael Hobbes' takedown of the BMI's dubious origins went viral and earned an Apple Episode of the Year nod.

title: The People in the Neighborhood
why: A New York Times culture conversation from Wesley Morris and Jenna Wortham that Apple chose as one of the best episodes of 2021.

title: The Symphony
why: The Talib Kweli, yasiin bey and Dave Chappelle salon at its most freewheeling, singled out by Apple and on The Atlantic's best of the year.

title: The Unwritten Rules of Black TV
why: An Atlantic/WNYC episode on the unspoken pressures surrounding Black television, named an Apple Episode of the Year for 2021.

title: This Strange Story
why: An installment of Dan Taberski's series on how 9/11 changed ordinary lives; Apple picked it as a 2021 best episode and the show later won the Ambie for Podcast of the Year.

title: Prince Harry
why: Harry likened royal life to The Truman Show and a zoo, and the interview dominated tabloid and mainstream headlines for days.

title: Our Unlikely Friendship
why: The debut of the Barack Obama and Bruce Springsteen conversations on Spotify was one of the most-covered podcast launches of the year.

title: #1757 - Dr. Robert Malone, MD
why: Malone's vaccine claims prompted an open letter from hundreds of medical professionals and set off the Spotify misinformation fight that saw Neil Young pull his music.

title: #172 The Test Kitchen, Chapter 1
why: A series on Bon Appétit's toxic workplace backfired as former staff accused Reply All itself of similar problems, leading to two hosts' departures.
